label: 16 March 1926
title: Liquid fuel leaves the ground
text: Robert Goddard launches a gasoline-and-liquid-oxygen rocket in Auburn, Massachusetts. NASA records a 2.5-second flight: a small experiment that demonstrated liquid-propellant flight.
lesson: The engine sits above the fuel and oxidizer tanks—an arrangement Goddard believed would improve stability.

label: 3 October 1942
title: The A-4 succeeds in flight
text: The fourth A-4 test vehicle completes the programme’s first successful launch at Peenemünde. The weapon later known as the V-2 becomes a major step in large liquid-propellant rocketry.
lesson: This development belongs to the history of Nazi weapons and forced labour as well as engineering. Production exploited concentration-camp prisoners; its human cost must remain part of the account.

label: 4 October 1957
title: A satellite reaches Earth orbit
text: The Soviet Union launches Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite. The achievement turns orbital flight into a demonstrated capability and accelerates the US–Soviet space race.
lesson: Reaching orbit becomes a practical launch-system objective. This milestone is the satellite launch, not the start of rocket development.
sourceLabel: NASA · Dawn of the Space Age

label: 9 November 1967
title: Saturn V flies for the first time
text: Apollo 4 is the first Saturn V launch. Its objectives include rocket–spacecraft compatibility, stage separation, structural behaviour and Apollo re-entry systems. NASA reports that all mission objectives were achieved.
lesson: A launch vehicle must work as an integrated system: propulsion, structures, separation and spacecraft interfaces are tested together.
sourceLabel: NASA · First launch of Saturn V

label: 5 January 1972
title: A reusable transport system is approved
text: President Richard Nixon announces the decision to develop the Space Shuttle. The programme centres on a vehicle intended to make repeated journeys between Earth and orbit.
lesson: The eventual system combines an orbiter, an external tank and two solid rocket boosters. It is partially reusable: the external tank is not recovered for another flight.
sourceLabel: NASA · The Space Shuttle, overview and programme decision

label: 12 August 1977
title: Enterprise proves the unpowered landing
text: Enterprise makes its first independent flight during the Approach and Landing Tests. Released from its carrier aircraft, the prototype tests the Shuttle’s approach and landing behaviour before orbital flights begin.
lesson: Approach and landing were tested in the atmosphere before the Shuttle flew in orbit. Enterprise never flew in space.
sourceLabel: NASA · Enterprise and the Approach and Landing Tests

label: 12 April 1981
title: Columbia takes the Shuttle into space
text: John Young and Robert Crippen launch aboard Columbia on STS-1, the first orbital Space Shuttle mission. The flight brings the programme from atmospheric tests to a crewed orbital demonstration.
lesson: The orbiter’s runway landing is one part of a system that must also survive launch, orbital operations and atmospheric entry.
sourceLabel: NASA History · The Space Shuttle’s First Flight

label: 28 January 1986
title: Challenger and its crew are lost
text: Challenger is lost 73 seconds into flight with all seven crew members. The event becomes a defining break in the Shuttle programme’s history.
lesson: A development timeline must include failures and their consequences, not only successful launches. Follow NASA’s history collection for the investigation record.

label: 29 September 1988
title: Discovery returns the fleet to flight
text: Discovery launches on STS-26, the first Shuttle flight after Challenger. NASA’s mission history documents the preparation and return to flight.
lesson: Returning to flight is a separate development milestone, rather than a continuation that erases the preceding accident.
sourceLabel: NASA History · STS-26 return to flight

label: 1 February 2003
title: Columbia is lost during re-entry
text: Columbia and its seven crew members are lost during atmospheric re-entry, shortly before the scheduled landing. NASA’s history collection links the accident investigation and supporting records.
lesson: Safe orbital operations alone do not establish a safe mission. The return through the atmosphere remains part of the vehicle’s complete flight system.

label: 26 July 2005
title: Discovery flies the second return-to-flight mission
text: Discovery carries the STS-114 crew on the Shuttle programme’s return to flight after Columbia. This is Discovery’s second return-to-flight role, following STS-26 in 1988.
lesson: Discovery links two distinct recovery periods in the programme: the return after Challenger in 1988 and the return after Columbia in 2005.

label: 21 July 2011
title: Atlantis closes the Shuttle era
text: Atlantis lands at Kennedy Space Center to complete STS-135. NASA’s Shuttle fleet ends a programme of 135 missions spanning 30 years of orbital flight.
lesson: The Shuttle carried crews and cargo, supported satellite work and helped build the International Space Station. This date marks the final landing, not the final launch.

label: 30 March 2017
title: A flight-proven Falcon 9 launches SES-10
text: SES-10 launches on a previously flown Falcon 9 first stage. SES records the launch on 30 March; SpaceX identifies 2017 as its first reflight of an orbital-class rocket.
lesson: The milestone is reflight of the first-stage booster, not reuse of the entire launch vehicle. Recovery and reflight are different achievements.
extraLabel: SpaceX · Falcon Payload User’s Guide, reusability

label: 16 November 2022
title: SLS and Orion fly Artemis I
text: Artemis I launches the Space Launch System and uncrewed Orion spacecraft. NASA describes it as the first integrated flight test of SLS, Orion and Exploration Ground Systems.
lesson: This milestone tests a deep-space exploration system. It is a completed historical flight, not a forecast of later Artemis missions.
